A grid can use three distinct roles at once: a dominant nonzero background, zero-valued target canvas cells, and a sparse nonzero motif color. Avoid assuming that zero is the background or that a particular numeric color is reserved.

## Inference and implementation

1. Identify the dominant background and candidate motif color using the full grid and spatial evidence. The motif may be disconnected from other objects, and its source cells may be a small fraction of the grid.
2. Gather all cells of the candidate motif color, including disconnected pieces. Normalize their coordinates relative to the motif bounding-box top-left. Preserve all holes within that box; the motif is the exact set of colored offsets, not a filled rectangle.
3. Search all in-bounds translations of those offsets. A target is eligible when each offset lands on a zero cell. Other cells inside the motif bounding box need not be zero unless demonstrations establish that requirement.
4. Stamp only the motif's colored offsets using the motif color. Preserve the source and unrelated grid cells unless a demo shows otherwise.
5. Validate exact full-grid equality against every demonstration before submitting. Test especially for overlapping candidate placements and positions where zero targets may be adjacent to source or background-colored cells.

## Common mistake

Do not use a generic scan that excludes assumed constants such as `(0, 5)` to find colors or then stamp the entire motif bounding box. Infer the colors from the current grid, distinguish target zeros from background, and stamp only the occupied motif offsets. A template that only approximately matches target holes is not evidence of a match; require every motif offset to land on a valid target cell.

# Sequential learning from costly ARC demonstrations

Apply when an ARC stream permits incremental demo requests and each request has a score cost.

## Evidence cycle

1. Before requesting a demo, name at least two live candidate rules and a concrete feature on which their predictions differ. Explain internally why the next pair could reveal that feature. Do not request merely because uncertainty exists; a request should have a plausible information target.
2. On receipt, inspect the complete pair immediately. Record exact changed cells `(row, col, before, after)`, verify dimensions, and note unchanged lookalike structures as negative evidence.
3. Update candidate rules against all available pairs, not just the newest one. Mark which hypotheses are contradicted, which survive, and what ambiguity remains. Do not issue consecutive demo requests without this analysis.
4. If a pair did not discriminate the candidates, reassess whether another request can realistically target the distinction. When no credible targeted example is apparent, stop probing and act on the best-supported model; avoid spending the demo budget on repeated open-ended requests.
5. After selecting a rule, implement it generally and run it on complete fixtures for every received pair. Compare outputs exactly before submitting the program-produced test grid.

## Cost discipline

A demo costs one attempt, and an unsolved instance can incur the full budget. Weigh the information value of a request against both that cost and the opportunity to submit. Prefer a prompt evidence-based decision when existing demos sufficiently constrain the transformation.

## Pitfalls

- Treating each new pair as an invitation to request yet another, without evaluating its information value.
- Asking broadly when the competing hypotheses do not predict a useful observable difference.
- Over-indexing on one changed cell while ignoring the rest of the pair and unchanged candidates.
- Claiming validation without executing the candidate on all complete supplied pairs.
